A_target.statement:
Let $Z: \closedint {p_L} {p_H} \to \R$ be the [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]] [[Definition:Excess Demand|excess demand]] of a single-good market with $\map Z {p_L} > 0 > \map Z {p_H}$.
Then there exists $p^* \in \openint {p_L} {p_H}$ such that:
:$\map Z {p^*} = 0$

B_source.statement:
Let $f: \closedint a b \to \R$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]].
Then $f$ attains every value between $\map f a$ and $\map f b$.

substitutions.the continuous function on an interval: excess demand as a function of price

derived.the sign change over the interval: excess supply at high prices and excess demand at low ones
derived.the point where the function vanishes: the price at which supply and demand balance

object_map.reformulation: Recast balancing supply and demand as a zero of excess demand, that is, a value attained by a continuous function.

validity_conditions: Excess demand must be continuous in price, which requires the underlying demand and supply to vary continuously and rules out discrete goods.
The sign condition at the two ends is what supplies the two bracketing values the theorem requires.
Only existence follows, not uniqueness: excess demand may cross zero several times unless it is monotone in price.
proof_plan: Model excess demand as a [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous function]] $Z$ of price on $\closedint {p_L} {p_H}$.
By the [[Intermediate Value Theorem]], since $0$ lies between these values, there exists $p^*$ with $\map Z {p^*} = 0$.
